extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of administrative law, political science, and public policy; researchers studying rulemaking, lobbying, and public comment influence
extracted.subtask_description: Operationalizing and modeling how public pressure (mass comments) and coalition characteristics relate to coalition- and organization-level lobbying success in U.S. federal rulemaking. Includes hand-coding of comment demands, coalition construction, and statistical modeling choices (OLS, Poisson mediator models, difference-in-differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying success (dependent variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand-coded on an interval from 2 (total success; the policy changed as requested) to -2 (total loss; the policy changed in the opposite direction requested).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate success by comparing the coalition’s requested policy outcomes to the final rule text; where requests include both substantive and procedural demands, prioritize substantive demands. Examples: NRDC coalition coded as 1 ('some desired changes'); PM Group coalition coded as -1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure campaign (binary indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator for whether the coalition used a public pressure campaign, i.e., mobilized mass comments (by definition, more than 99 mass comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base model (Equation 3.3) uses this binary indicator; alternative specifications use continuous measures of number of comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of mass comments (continuous measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Total number of form-letter public comments that a lobbying coalition mobilized; used as logged, linear, and quadratic terms in different models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models use either the logged number of comments (one additional comment matters more for smaller campaigns), a quadratic term to capture non-linear marginal effects, or rescaled counts (e.g., hundreds of thousands). Results may differ across specifications; some models find negative effects until very large campaigns (~1 million) then positive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition size
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of the number of distinct organizations lobbying together on the rule (unique commenting organizations in each coalition). For organizations lobbying alone, coalition size is 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coalition size correlated with lobbying success; when excluding single-organization coalitions, coalition size’s correlation with success weakens. When the same company sent multiple comments (e.g., franchised businesses), coalition size counts unique organizations only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition indicator (lobbying in coalition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary indicator for whether the organization is lobbying in a coalition (takes value 0 when coalition size is 1 and 1 if coalition size > 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in models to distinguish solo organizations from coalition members; members-of-Congress counts are defined only for coalitions >1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition unopposed
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition is unopposed when no opposing organizations comment on the same rule; derived from the hand-coded spatial position of each comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple coalitions support (or oppose) a rule for different reasons, a rule may have multiple unopposed lobbying coalitions. Include as a predictor in models (controls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition type: public vs private interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of coalitions as primarily public interest or private interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some models use this classification (public interest is compared to private interest as omitted category). Public interest coalitions are found to be much less successful than private interest coalitions in these data; interactions with pressure campaigns are included in some specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business coalition (binomial)
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition is coded as a business coalition if the majority of commenting organizations are for-profit businesses and trade associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an alternative, more objective coalition-type measure; alternative models use the number and share of businesses in a coalition instead. Interaction terms (Pressure Campaign × Business) are tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supports rule indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator for whether the organization/coalition supports the proposed rule (aligned with the direction of policy change proposed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strongest predictor of lobbying success across models—coalitions supporting the proposed rule have substantially higher success (e.g., ~1.27 points greater on the five-point scale in Model 1). Consider alignment with agency officials and selection of proposed rules that reach final publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding of substantive policy requests and mapping to final text
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand-coding of the specific policy demands in sophisticated comments (e.g., retain language, strengthen provisions, limit exemptions) and comparison of those demands to the final rule text to evaluate extent of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code specific requested outcomes (keywords/phrases) and then check whether final rule includes requested language or changes. Example: NRDC’s four substantive requests were used to search draft/final text and measure success as retention/partial adoption of requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of procedural/timing requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters sometimes request procedural outcomes (e.g., speedy publication, extended comment periods, delayed effective dates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hand-coding approach prioritizes change in policy text (substantive demands) when coding success; procedural or timing successes are captured but deprioritized if both substantive and procedural requests exist. This creates a bias toward zero in estimating public pressure effects if campaigns mainly achieve procedural outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and identification of coalitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Coalitions identified by linking organizations responsible for mobilizing comments; methods allow measurement per organization and per coalition and link common efforts by multiple organizations lobbying in broader coalitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include hand-coding and text reuse across dozens of federal agencies; this avoids treating one coalition’s campaign as many organization-level campaigns (avoids non-independence of observations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-independence and unit-of-analysis choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that organization-level counts can create non-independent observations when multiple organizations are part of the same coalition; using the coalition as the unit of analysis avoids counting one coalition as many campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previous studies counted organization campaigns (leading to many near-duplicate observations). This design measures public pressure and lobbying success at both organization and coalition levels and uses appropriate aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional support mediator (members of Congress comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of supportive comments from members of Congress is modeled as a mediator between public pressure campaigns and lobbying success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediator modeled with Poisson regression (count DV) because dispersion parameter not significantly above 1; outcome model includes member-of-Congress counts to estimate ACME and ADE via mediation analysis (Imai et al. 2010). Results show modest correlation but limited evidence of mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling strategy: OLS with fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Main relationship between public pressure and coalition-level lobbying success is estimated with OLS regression including agency and president fixed effects (𝛾_j + 𝛿_p) and control covariates X_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controls include coalition unopposed, coalition size, coalition type, support/opposition indicator. Standard errors clustered by agency in coalition-level models. Multiple specifications (binary pressure indicator, logged counts, quadratic) are compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling strategy: difference-in-differences at organization level
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare an organization’s lobbying success when it participates in pressure campaigns vs when it does not, using organization fixed effects (𝛼_i) to control for time-invariant organization characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equation 3.6: includes organization fixed effects, agency or rule fixed effects, and coalition- and organization-level covariates. This limits sample to organizations that lobby on multiple policies and helps isolate within-organization variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical data structure and dependence correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Data are hierarchical: comment-level observations nested within organization, within coalition, within rule, within agency, within administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combination of fixed and random effects to account for dependence among higher-level observations; roll data up to coalition level for main models; cluster standard errors appropriately (agency or org_name depending on model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonlinear specification choices for mass comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Models test logged term and quadratic term for number of mass comments to capture different marginal effects (e.g., diminishing returns or threshold effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: one additional comment matters more for smaller campaigns; Models 5 and 6 suggest relationship is negative until very large campaigns (~1 million comments) then positive. Compare results across specifications to assess robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediator model choice: Poisson for member-of-Congress counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the dependent mediator (number of supportive comments from members of Congress) is a count and dispersion parameter is not significantly above 1, a Poisson model is used for the mediator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate mediator as function of pressure campaign and covariates (Equation 3.4), then include mediator in outcome model (Equation 3.5) and compute ACME/ADE for mediation analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion rules for mediator models
rubrics_metrics.description: By definition, only coalitions with more than one organization have members of Congress in their coalition; thus 'coalitions' of 1 organization are excluded from mediator models and the coalition indicator is omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also subtract number of members of Congress from coalition size when modeling to avoid double-counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations to interpretability (bias toward zero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two main limitations bias estimates of public pressure campaign influence toward zero: (1) lobbying success may take forms other than changes in policy text (timing, extending comment period, delaying effective dates) and hand-coding prioritizes substantive text changes; (2) bureaucrats may anticipate public pressure campaigns when writing draft rules, muting observed relationships at the final rule stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge these limitations when interpreting null or weak effects; consider alternative outcomes (timing/procedural) and potential pre-policy anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescaling, sample design, and statistical power considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample includes random sample of agency rules with hand-coded comments; models use binary indicators, logged values, quadratic terms, and rescaling (e.g., hundreds of thousands) for mass comments. Small sample size limits power for some estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results may be sensitive to sample composition (oversample of high-salience rules) and lack of power produces wide confidence intervals for some coefficients; report R-squared, log-likelihood, and clustered SEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrative case examples for coding guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide worked examples of coding and numeric coding values for specific coalitions to illustrate coding rules (e.g., NRDC coalition: lobbying success=1, coalition size=15, business=0, position=supports rule=1, campaign=1, mass comments=943,931; PM Group coalition: success=-1, coalition size=129, business coalition=1, mass comments=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these examples to demonstrate how substantive requests are identified, how mass comments relate to sophisticated recommendations, and how coding decisions translate into model inputs.
